findings.title: Session-file escaping is promised globally but scoped only to selected vendor renderers
findings.why: A crafted session containing a round title, provider label, or other interpolated field such as `` can still execute in the webview if those fields are rendered outside the named reviewer and spending-row paths.
findings.fix: Inventory every session-derived interpolation in panelView and escape or DOM-text-render each one; add a regression test for a malicious value in each distinct rendered field.

findings.title: Removing a round from the auto-open set does not specify how later refreshes honor a person closing it
findings.why: If auto-open runs whenever a running round is absent from `expanded`, a person can close an auto-opened running round and then have it reopen on the next polling/update cycle, violating the promised closed state.
findings.fix: Define and implement a user-closed suppression state (or transition-only auto-open logic) that lasts while the round remains running, and test multiple refreshes after the close.

findings.title: The plan does not cover or verify vendor colouring in the round cards and live section it explicitly promises
findings.why: A vendor name rendered by a separate round-card or live-section path can remain grey even though reviewer and spending rows use `vendorColour`, so the stated cross-panel colour guarantee is false.
findings.fix: Identify every vendor-name rendering path, route each through the shared renderer/function, and add assertions for round cards, live rows, reviewer rows, and spending rows.

findings.title: Colour identity is based on an unspecified raw name rather than a canonical vendor identity
findings.why: If one source returns `Gemini` and another returns `gemini ` or a differently cased alias, hashing the displayed strings assigns different colours to the same vendor, breaking the cross-location guarantee.
findings.fix: Define a canonicalization/identity rule (at least trimming and case normalization, with alias handling if applicable) before hashing while preserving the preferred display name.

findings.title: Single reviewer row renderer producing HTML breaks existing text-based test assertions
findings.why: The plan requires a single shared renderer for reviewer rows to avoid drift ('The text version is what the tests read today'), but step 5 modifies this renderer to output HTML (<span class="vendor" style="...">). Existing tests asserting raw text reviewer strings will receive HTML tags and fail.
findings.fix: Explicitly update the test assertions to match the HTML output or separate the string composition from HTML decoration so both text tests and the HTML view have unambiguous contracts.

findings.title: Vendor colour indexing without case normalization produces mismatched colours for the same vendor
findings.why: Round cards and logs use lowercased identifiers (e.g. 'codex') while spending rows and provider configurations frequently use capitalized names (e.g. 'Codex'). If vendorColour computes an index from the raw string, the same vendor gets assigned different theme colours across views, violating Requirement 4.
findings.fix: Normalize the vendor string (e.g. name.trim().toLowerCase()) before indexing into the chart palette in vendorColour.

findings.title: Finished rounds auto-close without verifying ownership origin
findings.why: The plan states 'A round that finishes closes itself if it was this panel that opened it' but relies on a set that is 'pruned to living rounds'. If a user manually closes a round (removing it from the 'opened' set) while it is still running, and then the round finishes, the logic will see it as 'not in the opened set' and fail to close it, OR if the logic assumes 'not in the set' means 'person opened it', it will incorrectly close a round the user manually closed. Specifically: User opens Round A -> Panel tracks it. User manually closes Round A (removes from tracking). Round A finishes. The system sees Round A is finished but not in the 'opened' set. Depending on the exact implementation of 'if it was this panel that opened it', it might leave it open (leaving a ghost) or close it (hiding user's manual state). The plan lacks the mechanism to distinguish 'user closed' from 'never opened'.
findings.fix: Add a persistent state check (e.g., a timestamp or 'last_closed' flag) to the round object before auto-closing, ensuring the panel only closes rounds it explicitly opened.

findings.title: Ownership state for rounds is ephemeral and lost on restart
findings.why: The plan requires 'A round the person opened stays open when it finishes' and 'A running round the person closed stays closed'. The 'Build order' step 3 mentions 'A second set — the rounds THIS panel opened'. If this set is purely in-memory (as implied by 'pruned to living rounds' and lack of persistence mention), a restart of the VS Code extension will lose the history of which rounds were opened by the panel vs the user. Upon restart, the system will treat all currently open rounds as 'person opened' (since the panel's set is empty), causing it to incorrectly preserve their state or fail to auto-close them when they finish.
findings.fix: Define a persistent storage key for 'opened_by_panel' state that survives extension host restarts, rather than relying on in-memory sets that are 'pruned to living rounds'.

findings.title: Vendor color stability relies on undefined palette behavior
findings.why: The plan mandates 'Every vendor name renders in a colour that is stable for that vendor... and stable across restarts, since it is derived from the name rather than from the order rows arrive in.' It also says 'The colours come from the editor's own chart palette'. If the editor's chart palette (`--vscode-charts-*`) has fewer colors than the number of unique vendors, or if the palette is theme-dependent and the theme changes mid-session, the deterministic index into a 'fixed palette' might map to a different visual color or run out of colors, breaking the 'stable' requirement. Specifically: User has 10 vendors. Theme A has 5 colors. Theme B has 8 colors. The 'fixed palette' logic might fail to map 10 vendors to 5 colors consistently, or the 'stable across restarts' claim fails if the palette is re-evaluated on restart and the order of colors changes.
findings.fix: Explicitly define the color palette source and ensure the `vendorColour` function handles the case where the palette is empty or the theme changes dynamically.

findings.title: Fable command assumes immediate availability without fallback
findings.why: The plan removes the `FableAvailable` check and relies solely on the switch. If the Fable model is temporarily down (network issue, service restart) at the exact moment the user clicks 'Split with Fable', the command will fail silently or throw an error without the safety net of the previous check. The user expects the action to work, but the system has no way to verify the model is actually ready to receive the order, leading to a 'ghost' command that appears to be issued but fails.
findings.fix: Add a timeout or retry mechanism for the 'Split with Fable' command if the Fable model is temporarily unavailable, rather than assuming it is always available.

findings.title: Escaping and color mapping for special characters not explicitly tested
findings.why: The test plan mentions 'A reviewer row escapes a vendor name containing <'. However, it does not explicitly test the interaction between escaping and the color mapping. If a vendor name is `<script>` and the color is derived from the name, the escaping might alter the string used for the color index, causing the color to be inconsistent or the HTML to break. Specifically: Vendor name is `<script>`. The system escapes it to `<script>` for display. If the color index is calculated on the escaped string, it will differ from the color calculated on the raw string, breaking the 'stable' requirement.
findings.fix: Add a specific test case for the scenario where a vendor name contains a special character that might break the color mapping or the HTML escaping.

findings.title: Synchronous retry backoff stalls reviewer progress saves
findings.why: If the destination is briefly locked, each save sleeps 20+40+60+80 ms synchronously before succeeding. A nine-reviewer round with contention on each transition can delay progress by roughly 1.8 seconds, so the panel continues showing stale status while the persistence thread is blocked.
findings.fix: Use asynchronous delays or serialize/coalesce per-session saves so transient file contention does not block the round's progress path.

findings.title: Session save retry loop may block indefinitely on persistent file locks
findings.why: The `MoveOverExisting` method retries 5 times with exponential backoff (20ms, 40ms, 60ms, 80ms, 100ms). If a file lock (e.g., from an antivirus scanner or Windows Indexer) persists longer than the total retry window (~250ms) or if the lock is held by a process that doesn't release it quickly, the operation will fail. While the code allows the last attempt to throw, the lack of a hard time limit means the server could hang waiting for a transient lock if the retry logic is insufficient for the specific OS environment, potentially stalling the round progress reporting.
findings.fix: Ensure the `MoveOverExisting` retry loop uses a bounded, non-infinite timeout or a maximum total duration, rather than just a fixed number of attempts with increasing sleep intervals, to prevent indefinite blocking if the destination file is held by a long-running process (e.g., an antivirus scanner or indexer) that never releases it.

findings.fix: Move the `File.Delete(temp)` call inside the `try` block of the `Save` method, or ensure `TryDelete` is called in a `finally` block that executes even if `MoveOverExisting` throws on the final attempt.

findings.why: When two eligible processes share an unwritable data directory, neither can persist a claim; if both fail open as required, both issue the split command, violating the stated guarantee.

findings.title: The plan does not define crash recovery between claiming and issuing the command
findings.why: If a process persists the claim and is killed before launching the command, a retry suppresses the only command; if it launches the command and dies before persisting the claim, a retry issues it twice.
findings.fix: Specify an outbox/idempotency protocol or explicitly choose at-most-once versus at-least-once semantics, including recovery of an in-progress claim.

findings.title: Sessionless callers have no defined identity that can survive branch changes without conflating checkouts
findings.why: A caller without CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID can invoke on branch A, switch to branch B, and invoke again, while another process uses the same repository or a separate worktree; the plan provides no stable checkout key or rules to distinguish these cases, so orders can be lost or incorrectly shared.

findings.title: The caller-id filename constraint lacks a collision-safe representation
findings.why: Raw or ad hoc sanitization can turn distinct ids such as `a/b` and `a_b` into the same file, while ids such as `..` or very long values can escape intended semantics or exceed filesystem limits, causing one caller to suppress another or access an unintended path.

findings.title: The plan does not establish how the command is tied to the verdict from this review round
findings.why: If a prior round passed and the resolve loop changes the plan, or a stale verdict is read from persisted state, the caller can issue a split command for text that was not reviewed and passed in the current round.
findings.fix: Carry an immutable current-round plan digest together with the verdict and require that exact digest at command-claim time; specify rejection when it differs.

findings.title: SCOPE — Long-lived caller sessions permanently suppress splitting on subsequent independent plans
findings.why: CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID remains constant for the entire lifetime of an interactive Claude Code session across multiple user prompts and tasks. Once a first plan splits and claims the session ID, any subsequent, unrelated large plan created later in the same Claude session will match the claimed session ID and be incorrectly forced into the single-unit autonomy path.
findings.fix: Key the split claim by a combination of the caller session ID and the root plan's hash or unique identifier instead of session ID alone.

findings.title: What must be true (Item 5) — Failing open on unwritable storage restores infinite recursive epic splitting
findings.why: When the backing store is unwritable (e.g., read-only filesystem or restricted permissions), failing open allows review rounds to proceed without persisting claims. Child epics returning on new branches will find no recorded claim and will be repeatedly commanded to split into sub-epics without floor.
findings.fix: Fail closed on unwritable storage by defaulting to the single-unit autonomy order or in-memory tracking with a warning rather than re-issuing split orders.

findings.title: What must be true (Item 6) — Checkout-level fallback collides across independent runs in the same workspace
findings.why: For callers that export no session ID, tracking across branches of one checkout requires shared checkout-level state. Subsequent runs on the same checkout will observe the prior run's claim, causing future top-level plans in that checkout to bypass splitting entirely.
findings.fix: Derive identity from caller process tree lineage (PPID) or transient run tokens rather than static repository checkout identity when session ID is absent.

findings.title: Atomic claim across processes relies on transient environment variables rather than persistent state.
findings.why: Constraint 4 states 'two servers sharing a data directory cannot both give it' based on an atomic claim. However, Constraint 7 and the 'What must be true' section rely on `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` being exported to children. If Server A spawns a child process that splits the plan, and Server B (or a different instance of Server A) starts a new process in the same directory before the first child finishes or before the session ID is written to a persistent store, both may read the same 'unclaimed' state. Specifically, if the 'claim' is only held in memory or a transient env var, a restart of the child process or a race condition where two processes read the directory simultaneously will result in both servers issuing split orders for the same epic, causing duplicate work and conflicting commits.
findings.fix: Explicitly define the 'caller' as a persistent process ID or a shared lock file in the data directory, rather than relying on an environment variable passed to child processes.

findings.title: No mechanism exists to verify the 'floor' for splitting epics of epics.
findings.why: The plan promises 'no epics of epics, with no floor' (Scope section) and that a caller is ordered to split ONCE. However, the mechanism described relies on the 'caller' crossing sessions. If the 'caller' (the parent process) is killed or times out after issuing the split command but before the child process completes its review, the child process (now a 'caller' for its own sub-epics) may re-evaluate the plan. Without a persistent counter or a 'depth' flag written to the plan file itself, the child process might re-apply the split logic to its own output, creating an infinite recursion of 'epics of epics' because the 'floor' is only a logical concept in the text, not a verified state in the system.
findings.fix: Add a persistent 'split depth' counter to the plan state file that is incremented on every split and checked before issuing a new split command.

findings.title: Silent feature disablement on unwritable store leads to undetected state drift.
findings.why: Constraint 5 states an unwritable store fails OPEN with a warning rather than silently disabling. If the store is unwritable due to a disk full error or permission change, the system logs a warning but continues. If the 'split' logic relies on writing the 'session ID' or 'split depth' to this store to prevent re-splitting (as implied by the need for a floor), the system will proceed to split again on the next run because the state wasn't persisted. This results in the system repeatedly splitting the same plan into smaller and smaller units, eventually hitting the 'floor' (or lack thereof) and causing a cascade of tiny, unmanageable tasks.
findings.fix: Define a specific timeout and retry strategy for the 'OPEN' failure in Constraint 5, and ensure the 'warning' is logged to a persistent audit trail, not just stdout.

findings.title: Missing session ID causes silent failure or incorrect branching logic.
findings.why: Constraint 6 states 'A client that exports no session id is still followed across the branches of one checkout.' If a user manually triggers a split (e.g., via a CLI flag) without the `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` being set (perhaps because they ran the command in a shell where the variable wasn't exported), the system assumes it is a 'new' session. It will treat the plan as a 'caller' that hasn't been split yet, potentially re-splitting a plan that was already split in a previous session, or failing to link the child branch back to the parent, breaking the 'crossing' logic described in the Scope section.
findings.fix: Add a step to verify the 'caller' ID matches the current session ID before processing the split, or explicitly handle the case where the ID is missing.

findings.title: Caller ID escaping the directory creates potential for cross-project contamination.
findings.why: Constraint 4 states 'A caller id is somebody else's string and reaches a file name: it must not escape the directory.' If the `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` contains a path separator (e.g., `user/repo/branch`) or a special character, and the system uses it directly as a filename without sanitization, it could create a file structure like `data/user/repo/branch/split.lock`. findings.fix: Add a validation step that checks the 'caller' ID against the directory name or a lock file before allowing the split to proceed.

findings.fix: Handle only the expected `CreateNew` name-collision as an already-claimed result; let write and other I/O failures reach the warning-and-return-true path.

findings.title: Expired claims are renewed with a delete-then-create race
findings.why: Two servers can both observe an expired claim, then one can delete the newly recreated file after the other has created it; both `TryClaimSplitOrder` calls return true and both issue the split order.
findings.fix: Serialize expiry replacement with a per-caller lock or use an atomic OS-level replace protocol; do not delete the claim outside that serialization.

findings.title: Write failures can be mistaken for a successful competing claim and fail closed
findings.why: If `CreateNew` succeeds but the subsequent write fails, such as a full disk, the file exists, so the filtered IOException handler returns false without warning. The caller with the order is therefore told not to split, violating the fail-open requirement and potentially leaving an unusable claim file.
findings.fix: Distinguish an IOException from `CreateNew` caused by an existing file from exceptions during stream creation or writing; warn and return true for write failures.

findings.title: Unconditional File.Delete before FileMode.CreateNew creates a race condition allowing concurrent callers to both claim the split order
findings.why: When two processes concurrently invoke TryClaimSplitOrder for an unclaimed or expired caller, both pass StillRemembered as false. Process A reaches File.Delete and opens the file with FileMode.CreateNew, successfully creating the claim file and closing it. Process B, having already evaluated StillRemembered as false, executes File.Delete(file) immediately after, deleting Process A's newly established claim. Process B then successfully creates the file via FileMode.CreateNew and also returns true. Both callers believe they claimed the order and both issue split orders, defeating cross-process atomicity.
findings.fix: Do not delete the existing file before attempting FileMode.CreateNew; attempt atomic creation first and only handle file cleanup/replacement if the file on disk is confirmed expired.

findings.title: Unwritable caller session store emits warning on every single claim attempt without recovery or clear resolution guidance
findings.why: When the data directory is unwritable or permissions fail, every split-eligible plan review triggers an IOException/UnauthorizedAccessException and emits a warning log for each round. The log string describes the symptom and says 'the order is being given, and may be given again', but does not inform the developer/operator what path failed or how to resolve the directory permission issue, cluttering logs on every round.
findings.fix: Include actionable remediation in the log message (e.g., directory path and permission check guidance) or cache the unwritable state/back off logging so repeated rounds on an unwritable directory do not spam duplicate unresolvable warnings.

findings.title: File.Exists check before File.Delete introduces a redundant disk metadata roundtrip on the hot claim path

findings.fix: Remove the `if (File.Exists(file))` guard and call `File.Delete(file)` directly inside the try block.

findings.title: Atomic claim race condition due to pre-check file deletion outside the critical section
findings.why: The code checks `StillRemembered` (line 93), then deletes the file (line 97), then attempts `FileMode.CreateNew` (line 100). If a second server deletes the file between the check and the delete, or if the delete fails silently, the `CreateNew` might fail or succeed unexpectedly. More critically, if the file exists but is locked by another process, `File.Delete` might throw or hang, causing the `CreateNew` to fail or the method to return false incorrectly. The race window is widened by the explicit delete before the atomic write.
findings.fix: Move the `File.Delete(file)` call inside the `try` block, immediately after the `StillRemembered` check, or wrap the delete in its own try-catch to ensure the atomic `CreateNew` is not blocked by a stale file handle or race condition.

findings.title: FileStream options not optimized for sequential, low-frequency writes
